title: Dell's Multiple Falls On Servers It Cannot Build Fast Enough
detail:
Dell's Multiple Falls On Servers It Cannot Build Fast Enough
Trefis Team
Thu, August 27, 2026 at 11:40 AM PDT 4 min read
DELL
HPQ
IBM
HPE
AAPL
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by ArtsyBee on Pixabay

The forward valuation looks like a discount, but what closes it is low-margin server volume, and consensus already sits above what management guided.

Dell Technologies (DELL) has returned 258.5% over the past twelve months. A run like that leaves a stock looking expensive, and at roughly 35.5 times trailing adjusted earnings it does. The forward arithmetic disagrees, and what closes the gap is not a cheaper stock but a particular kind of growth.

The Multiple Is 40% Lower By Fiscal 2028

Analysts expect enough growth from those adjusted, non-GAAP earnings that the same price is about 24.5 times fiscal 2027 and 21.4 times fiscal 2028, a 40% lower multiple with no help from the price. One caveat: the trailing figure adds stock-based compensation back to normalized income to sit nearer the consensus basis, but the two adjusted measures are not defined identically, so part of the fall is definition, not earnings.

AI Servers Bring The Growth At A Lower Target Margin

Consensus needs earnings growing about 33.7% a year from the trailing twelve months to fiscal 2028. Most of that comes from margin expansion in the nearer term: from the trailing twelve months to fiscal 2027, earnings are expected to outgrow revenue. From fiscal 2027 to fiscal 2028, though, earnings and revenue are expected to move at a similar pace, so margins are assumed to hold flat, not climb further. The growth arrives as AI servers, for which management targets a mid-single-digit operating income rate, below the 10.5% ISG, the server and storage business, delivered in fiscal Q1 2027. That ISG rate was up 80 basis points even as AI servers grew nearly 800% year over year; scale has kept the company's margin up so far.

Consensus, however, assumes that dynamic doesn't continue: it's modeling flat margins from here, not further expansion, as AI servers become a larger share of the mix. The full-year outlook leans the same way, asking ISG to grow roughly 80% on $60 billion of AI server revenue at the midpoint, while CSG, the PC business, grows low teens. Growth concentrated in one build-out is a different proposition from the Trefis High Quality Portfolio, which does not depend on the handful of largest technology names to produce its returns.

Consensus Asks For Less Growth Than Dell Delivered, And More Profit Than Dell Guided

The forecast is not aggressive. Revenue grew 38.6% over the trailing twelve months, while consensus averages about 25.6% a year from there through fiscal 2028. Where consensus reaches is on profit: analysts carry about $18.89 a share for fiscal 2027, above the $17.90, plus or minus $0.25, that management guided on its own non-GAAP basis at the fiscal Q1 2027 call. The limit is not the order book: Dell exited fiscal Q1 2027 with a record $51.3 billion of AI backlog. Management has said it is supply constrained in the back half of fiscal 2027, not demand constrained, with DRAM, NAND and CPUs the parts it is chasing.

Cisco Systems: The January, April, July, October Anchor

Cisco Systems (NASDAQ:CSCO) writes checks in January, April, July, and October, making it the natural first leg of this 12-month bundle. The quarterly payout is $0.42 per share, with an annualized forward dividend of $1.68 and a yield of 1.49% at a share price of $112.

In terms of recent results, Cisco generated $5.4 billion of operating cash flow in Q4 alone and closed FY26 with $15.9 billion in cash and investments. Management returned $12.7 billion to shareholders in fiscal 2026, split between $6.6 billion in cash dividends and $6.1 billion of share repurchases, which CEO Chuck Robbins pegged at 99% of free cash flow. The track record: Cisco "increased our dividend for the 15th consecutive year in FY26."

The bull case for income investors is that the payout is being financed by an AI networking upcycle rather than a slow-growth cash cow. FY26 revenue hit $63.3 billion, up 12%, and FY27 guidance calls for revenue of $72.2 billion to $73.4 billion with non-GAAP EPS of $5.05 to $5.11. That gives the $1.68 annualized dividend enormous coverage.

title: Why Is IonQ Stock Sinking?
detail:
Why Is IonQ Stock Sinking?
Trefis Team
Thu, August 27, 2026 at 9:17 AM PDT 4 min read
RGTI
QBTS
GOOG
IONQ
HON
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by ArtsyBee on Pixabay

Rigetti fell nearly as far over the same stretch while IBM and Honeywell held up far better, a split narrow enough to locate the move in how the quantum story is priced, not in anything IonQ reported.

IonQ (IONQ) shares fell 42.9% between late May and late August, from $70.14 to $40.03. The S&P 500 gained 1.5% over the same stretch. The natural assumption is that the company's immediate operational performance deteriorated. Yet IonQ's reported quarterly results showed continued commercial execution. Inside that same window the company posted the strongest quarter in its history, raised its full-year revenue guidance and closed a $1.8 billion acquisition.

Record Revenue Came From Machines Leaving The Building

Second-quarter revenue was $80.1 million, up 287% from a year earlier and up 132% on an organic basis, and management raised full-year guidance for IonQ alone to $280 million to $290 million. The largest piece of that upside was physical: the rollout of fifth-generation quantum computing systems, with subsystems shipped to KISTI in South Korea and a machine in final assembly at QuantumBasel, next to the fourth-generation machine that a customer bought earlier. A repeat buyer taking the next generation of machine is not the behavior of a market losing interest.

Rigetti Fell Almost As Far, IBM And Honeywell Did Not

Over the identical window Rigetti Computing fell 41.0%, within two points of IonQ, while IBM fell 12.4% and Honeywell International fell 5.9%. A decline that catches IonQ and Rigetti together is no verdict on one company's execution, and against a rising S&P 500 it is not a market-wide move either.

Concentrated heavily in pure-play names while diversified giants like IBM and Honeywell held up far better, the decline points at a repricing aimed at pure-play quantum valuations rather than broader tech. Returns that arrive and leave with a single thematic story are a different proposition from the Trefis High Quality Portfolio, which does not depend on the handful of largest technology names to produce its returns.

Owning The Foundry Did Not Come With Combined Numbers

One thing did deteriorate over those three months, and it came from the deal meant to reduce risk. IonQ closed its $1.8 billion acquisition of SkyWater days before reporting, putting a semiconductor foundry under its own roof to fabricate the ion trap chips built for the electronic qubit control technology of Oxford Ionics, acquired in September 2025. The first fully featured, fully integrated chips from that foundry are under test at IonQ's College Park facility, with 256-qubit systems planned to begin commissioning in 2027. That pace is expensive well before it produces revenue. Adjusted EBITDA for the June quarter was negative $120.3 million, about $20 million of that additional SkyWater spending and roughly $10 million more in pre-integration costs. After less than a week as a combined company, and with roughly $120 million of IonQ's fiscal 2026 spending with SkyWater converting into SkyWater's own revenue, some of it still to be eliminated on consolidation, management has not yet guided the combined company at all.

title: Seagate (STX) Up 10.7% Since Last Earnings Report: Can It Continue?
detail:
Seagate (STX) Up 10.7% Since Last Earnings Report: Can It Continue?
Seagate (STX) Up 10.7% Since Last Earnings Report: Can It Continue? · Zacks
Zacks Equity Research
Thu, August 27, 2026 at 8:30 AM PDT 6 min read
STX
^GSPC
IBM
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

It has been about a month since the last earnings report for Seagate (STX). Shares have added about 10.7% in that time frame, outperforming the S&P 500.

But investors have to be wondering, will the recent positive trend continue leading up to its next earnings release, or is Seagate due for a pullback? Before we dive into how investors and analysts have reacted as of late, let's take a quick look at its most recent earnings report in order to get a better handle on the important catalysts.

Seagate's Q4 Earnings Beat Estimates

Seagate reported fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 non-GAAP earnings of $5.71 per share, beating the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $5.10 and exceeding the high end of management's guidance of $5 per share (+/- 20 cents). The bottom line also expanded a whopping 121% year over year.

Non-GAAP revenues of $3.6 billion surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 3.9%. Revenues were above the midpoint of guidance, increasing 48% year over year. Robust cloud spending and disciplined operational execution boosted the company's performance. Strong AI-driven demand for cloud storage solutions helped Seagate achieve 34% revenue growth in fiscal 2026 to $12.2 billion. With improving demand visibility, the company expects fiscal 2027 revenue growth to outpace that of fiscal 2026.

Strong enterprise OEM demand led to double-digit revenue and exabyte shipment growth in the June quarter. Seagate is expanding HAMR production to meet growing cloud and enterprise storage needs. It shipped 218 exabytes, up 34% year over year, with data centers accounting for 89% of total shipments. Data center exabyte shipments increased 43% year over year and 11% sequentially. Global cloud customers constitute the majority of Seagate's data center revenue and exabyte demand.

The company is expanding production of HAMR-based drives, initially targeting cloud customers before broadening adoption across enterprise markets. It is investing in manufacturing capacity and technology to support the transition while maintaining stable output as demand shifts to higher-capacity drives. These efforts are expected to support mid-20% annual nearline exabyte growth over the next few years.

Revenues by End Market

Beginning first-quarter fiscal 2026, it reports revenues across two key markets — Data Center, encompassing nearline products and systems sold to cloud, enterprise and VIA customers, and Edge IoT, covering consumer and client-focused segments, including network-attached storage.

The data center accounted for 81% of total revenues, at $2.9 billion, representing a 17% sequential increase and 57% year-over-year growth.

title: Can Oracle Stock Fund a $638B Backlog Without Breaking Margins?
detail:
Can Oracle Stock Fund a $638B Backlog Without Breaking Margins?
Trefis Team
Thu, August 27, 2026 at 7:37 AM PDT 3 min read
AMZN
MSFT
IBM
ORCL-PD
GOOG
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by StockSnap on Pixabay

The supply bottleneck management used to name has gone quiet, and what replaced it changes the kind of company you own.

Oracle (ORCL) used to tell investors that its cloud build was rationed by parts rather than by demand. That caveat has faded from the front of the story. In its place sits a construction program the company must fund before it can bill it. Same ticker, different bet: shares are down 36.0% over the past twelve months as the market weighs the sheer scale of the funding plan and near-term margin pressure against the surge in booked demand.

In Early 2025, The Limit Management Named Was Component Delays

Demand was running far ahead of supply, management said, and the component delays slowing cloud capacity expansion would ease. Components have not gone away, but they surface now as a cost question, not a capacity one: on rising memory and hard drive prices, management says its longer contracts pass the cost to customers instead of into margin.

Funding The Build Is The New Version Of Waiting For Parts

The size of the swap shows up in what customers have contracted for: $130 billion in early 2025, and $638 billion at the close of fiscal 2026. That book is not a queue waiting on parts; rather than naming a bottleneck, management frames the massive capital program as fully pulled by committed customer demand—leaving the funding burden as the operational reality investors must now underwrite. The guided figure is a net cash outlay for capital expenditures of about $70 billion in fiscal 2027, with a funding plan of around $40 billion of debt and equity behind it. Both numbers sit against a company whose annual revenue first passed $67 billion in fiscal 2026. To own Oracle from here is to underwrite that construction program, a different proposition from the Trefis High Quality Portfolio, which does not depend on the handful of largest technology names to produce its returns.

The Delivered Gigawatts Suggest The Delays Eased

The quiet looks like a solved problem, not a dropped one. Oracle delivered more than 1.2 gigawatts of capacity to customers across fiscal 2026, and expects fiscal Q1 2027 alone to approach a gigawatt, close to what the previous four quarters delivered combined. A business still rationed by suppliers does not deliver most of a year's capacity in a quarter. The business under the silence is growing faster, not slower: revenue grew 17.4% over the trailing twelve months against a three-year average of 10.6%. Most of the AI infrastructure signed in fiscal Q4 2026 was prepaid or on a bring your own hardware basis. The $20 billion to $25 billion of customer prepayments and timing is why reported capital spending runs above the net outlay, so the $70 billion is the part Oracle funds itself.

title: Palantir Technologies Stock Surged On Evidence That Was Already Public
detail:
Palantir Technologies Stock Surged On Evidence That Was Already Public
Trefis Team

PLTR
^GSPC
STLA
CLF
SNOW
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by athree23 on Pixabay

The customers, the contracts, and the expansion rate behind Palantir's run were all on the record before the price moved, and the options market had stopped bracing for a big move.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR) stock returned 34% over the three months through late August, against 2.1% for the S&P 500. The August 3 second-quarter report got the credit. But nearly everything it confirmed had already been signed, filed or said out loud by early May. The run was legible in advance.

Stellantis, The USDA And Cleveland-Cliffs All Signed First

In late March the company renewed and expanded its Stellantis partnership for another five years, broadening Stellantis's use of Palantir Foundry and adding Palantir's AI platform. In April the USDA awarded a contract of up to $300 million to secure farmland and modernize its services to farmers, and Cleveland-Cliffs signed a three-year deal putting Palantir's AI at the center of its own operations and commercial processes. Trailing-twelve-month revenue as of fiscal Q1 2026 was $5.22 billion, so none of this was transformative alone; what mattered was that all three were agreed before the price moved.

The Expansion Rate Climbed Across Three Quarters

Contracts are lumpy. The cleaner tell was net dollar retention, which tracks what existing customers spend against a year earlier, excluding anyone won in the past twelve months. Retention ran 134% for fiscal Q3 2025 and 139% for fiscal Q4 2025, then jumped 1,100 basis points to 150% for fiscal Q1 2026, the largest step in that run and on the record in early May. That climb is not a forecast about AI; it is customers who already bought paying for more. The growth was profitable too: trailing operating margin as of fiscal Q1 2026 was 38.1%, against a three-year average of 14.2%. Growth arriving with margins like that is the combination the Trefis High Quality Portfolio looks for in its holdings.

AI Sovereignty Was A New Label On Old Momentum

The thesis predates August too. In early May the company's revenue chief framed the opportunity as enterprises waking up to the risk of being beholden to models alone. On August 3 that got a name and a number: U.S. commercial revenue up 149% year over year to $764 million in fiscal Q2 2026, and full-year 2026 revenue guidance raised to a midpoint of $8.154 billion, representing 82% growth year over year and an 11-point increase over the prior guide's growth rate. Management calls the demand "AI sovereignty," meaning customers who want their data, logic, and security under their own control, not an outside lab's. Demand kept arriving after fiscal Q2 2026 closed: the Sovereignty Bootcamps have drawn nearly 200 organizations, with a second announced on August 19.
